title: Roots never have nested digit sequences

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Roots never have nested digit sequences

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Nested digit sequences, such as those produced by substitution systems, never correspond to numbers obtainable by taking roots (square roots, cube roots, and so on).

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: such a digit sequence never corresponds to a number that can be obtained by the mathematical operation of taking roots.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 4, “Systems Based on Numbers”; section “Mathematical Constants” (from p. 136), p. 142. Scope: digit expansions of algebraic numbers obtained as roots

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch04-15: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.70

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Strong published results show transcendence for broad classes of nonperiodic automatic or low-complexity expansions. Without a precise substitution class, those results do not necessarily cover every pattern Wolfram calls nested.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Formalize nested sequences as outputs of a specified substitution class and roots as algebraic numbers, then apply or seek transcendence results for the resulting digit expansions. Existing theorems settle important classes; a single algebraic counterexample would refute the unrestricted statement.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Nested digit sequence is not a unique formal class.

Transcendence results differ across substitution families.

The unrestricted wording may exceed known theorems.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Roots of integers are algebraic, and a published theorem says an irrational number with an automatic base-b expansion is transcendental, so it is not such a root. Constant-length substitution systems, which are the nested digit sequences Wolfram constructs, produce automatic sequences, so the mapping is the standard one. The remaining care is whether every pattern he would call nested falls under that theorem; that is a scope check inside the proof, not a missing dataset.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Identify nested digit sequences from substitution systems with automatic or morphic sequences, and use the theorem that irrational automatic numbers are transcendental. An algebraic integer root whose digits are generated by such a substitution would refute the claim; the transcendence theorem confirms it for that class.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Wolfram's 'nested' has to be mapped onto automatic or morphic sequences, and non-constant-length substitutions are the less immediate case.

The theorem is specialist reading rather than a few days of routine checking.
